On-call handbook (draft)
========================

This document was written in a plain text editor with a hard wrap at 78
columns, so every paragraph is made of many short lines. Nothing here is
formatted with modern Markdown, which is exactly the point of the test.

Being on call
-------------

When you are on call you are the first person paged for any production
alert. You are not expected to fix everything yourself, but you are
expected to acknowledge within five minutes, to assess the impact, and to
pull in the right people when the problem is bigger than you can handle
alone. Write down what you do as you go, because the notes become the
timeline of the incident review.

Handover
--------

The handover happens on Monday at 10:00. The outgoing engineer writes a
short summary of anything that is still open, any alerts that were noisy,
and any changes that are scheduled for the coming week. The incoming
engineer reads it and asks questions before the call ends.

***

Escalation
----------

If you cannot reach the owner of a service within fifteen minutes, call the
engineering manager. If you cannot reach the manager, call the CTO. Do not
wait longer than fifteen minutes when customers are affected.
